subject: design-technology
title: Applications: JIT, JIC and Lean Manufacturing
welcome_lead: Tour a modern factory and see how Just-in-Time, Just-in-Case and lean methods cut waste while keeping shelves stocked.
meta_desc: Apply JIT, JIC and lean manufacturing strategies in real production contexts.
final_note: You can weigh up stock strategies and explain how lean thinking removes waste.

concepts.def: Materials arrive only when needed, cutting storage costs.
Holding extra stock to cover delays or demand spikes.
Removing waste to improve flow and value.
Spare inventory kept as a safety net.
Continuous small improvements made by workers.
Network of suppliers feeding a factory.

walkthroughs.body_html: JIT orders components to arrive exactly when needed. It cuts warehouse costs but breaks if a supplier is late. JIC stockpiles materials so production never stops, but ties up cash in storage. Toyota famously pioneered JIT in car assembly.

Lean identifies wastes such as overproduction, waiting, defects and excess stock. Tools include kaizen (small daily improvements), 5S (sort, set, shine, standardise, sustain) and value-stream mapping. The goal is to flow value to the customer with minimum waste.
A bike maker switches from JIC to JIT. Storage costs fall 40% but a port strike halts production for a week. The lesson: JIT needs reliable suppliers and a backup plan.

mcqs.q: Which strategy keeps extra stock as a safety net?

numericals.q: A factory cuts storage costs from £20,000 to £8,000. How much is saved?
